=== CALL C0015 ===
Tracey: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
Maricel: Hi, yes, I can hear you. Hi.
Tracey: Lovely. I'm Tracey. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was useless at it, honestly, I just sat there going round in circles.
Maricel: Erm, I'm Maricel. Yeah, I did it. I think I got stuck on the last one as well, so.
Tracey: Oh thank God, it's not just me then. I thought, they're gonna think I'm thick. So what do you do, Maricel? Sorry, am I saying that right?
Maricel: Yes, Maricel, that's right. Erm, I'm a pharmacy technician. In Leyton, a little independent pharmacy.
Tracey: Oh right, so like the one behind the counter doing the prescriptions?
Maricel: Sort of, yeah. I do the checking, so when the dispensing's done I check it's the right drug, right strength, right patient. And I do a lot for care homes, sorting out their medicines when people come out of hospital. It's quite fiddly but I like it, honestly. You have to be very careful.
Tracey: Ar, I bet. I couldn't do that, I'd be terrified of getting it wrong. I'm a fitness instructor, at the leisure centre in Walsall. Aqua aerobics, circuits, and I do a seated class for the older ones.
Maricel: Oh, seated exercise. That's nice. A lot of my care home patients would probably benefit from that, to be fair.
Tracey: They love it. I've got one lady, she's ninety-one, comes every Tuesday on the bus, never misses. Mind you, half of 'em come for the chat and the cup of tea after, not the exercise. Sorry, am I going on?
Maricel: No, no. That's lovely. I think that's important, the chat part. With the elderly patients, a lot of the time they just want someone to listen.
Tracey: That's it exactly.
Maricel: Mm.
Tracey: So is that all week then, the pharmacy?
Maricel: Three and a half days. I keep the rest for pottery, mostly. I do a wheel class every week.
Tracey: Oh, is that them mugs behind you in your photo? On the shelf? I noticed them when we was doing the pictures bit.
Maricel: Yes! Erm, yeah, those are mine. The blue speckled ones. I sell a few on Instagram, just small.
Tracey: Get away, you made them? They look like proper shop ones. I thought you'd bought them somewhere posh.
Maricel: Thank you. Honestly, the glaze is the hard part. You do a test tile and it comes out one colour, then the actual mug comes out completely different. The last batch was supposed to be green and it came out sort of brown. Like tea.
Tracey: Ha, well, I'd still drink out of it. I'm not arty at all, me. I'd make an ashtray by accident.
Maricel: Everyone says that, but it's mostly practice. You'd probably be good, you know, with the coordination and everything.
Tracey: Maybe. I don't get the time though, really. I've got my lad, Kieran, he's sixteen, so I'm forever driving him to football and feeding him. He eats me out of house and home.
Maricel: Sixteen. I can imagine.
Tracey: Two loaves a week, I'm not joking. And my mum's ten minutes up the road, so I'm back and forth there as well. Is your family near you?
Maricel: Erm, no. My mum's in Manila, in the Philippines. And my brother. I go every other year, for a month usually.
Tracey: Oh bless you, that's a long way. Do you miss her?
Maricel: Yeah. Yeah, I do. It's hard, she's getting older. You feel a bit guilty, you know, being here.
Tracey: I know what you mean. My mum's knee's playing up and I worry, and I'm only round the corner, so I can't imagine being all that way.
Maricel: Mm. It's okay. We video call a lot, like this.
Tracey: Well, that's something. And when you go over, do you just stay with her the whole month, or do you get to—

=== CALL C0016 ===
Lewis: Alright mate, how's it going?
Luke: Alright, yeah. Can you hear me okay?
Lewis: Yeah, loud and clear. I'm Lewis.
Luke: Luke. Nice one.
Lewis: Saw your photo. Southampton, yeah? With the team picture.
Luke: Yeah, that's me. My dad's fault, to be fair. You're Spurs, I saw the shirt.
Lewis: Guilty. Don't start, I know. We bottle it every year, it's tradition at this point.
Luke: I wasn't gonna say anything. We've got no room to talk, mate.
Lewis: Ha, fair. So what d'you do then?
Luke: Erm, I'm a shift manager at a parcel depot. In Basingstoke. Early shift, so about forty people, sorters and loaders.
Lewis: Early shift, what's that, like five?
Luke: I'm in for half five. So I'm sort of knackered by about Wednesday. By Friday I'm basically a zombie.
Lewis: Rather you than me, mate. I'd be useless.
Luke: What about you?
Lewis: I've got my own business, tiling. Bathrooms, kitchen floors, that kind of thing. Bishop's Stortford, round Harlow. Bit of everything really. Plan is to get a couple of lads under me, do full bathroom fits, get the name on the van, you know.
Luke: Oh, nice. Is it busy?
Lewis: Yeah, it's alright. Comes and goes. Mostly word of mouth, through my dad's mates and a builder I know. Don't really need to advertise, to be fair.
Luke: That's handy. Word of mouth's the best way, isn't it.
Lewis: Yeah, and you can sort of pick your hours. I don't do Wednesday nights, that's five-a-side.
Luke: I used to play. Stopped after my knee went a bit. Not properly went, just sort of twinged and I thought, yeah, I'm done.
Lewis: Knees, mate. Don't. Kneeling on floors all day, I reckon mine are gonna be shot by forty.
Luke: Yeah, that can't be good for you long term, can it.
Lewis: Nah. So what else, you do anything at the weekends?
Luke: Fishing, mostly. Carp. There's a couple of lakes near me, I go down on a Saturday and sit there all day. Caught a decent common last weekend actually, about eighteen pound. Bit quiet for most people, but it's sort of the only time I'm not thinking about work.
Lewis: Eighteen pound? That's a big fish. Do you eat 'em?
Luke: No, no, you put 'em back. Photo, back in. That's the whole thing.
Lewis: Mad. Sit there all day and then let it go. I'd get bored, I'm not gonna lie.
Luke: Everyone says that. My girlfriend thinks I'm mental. But it's peaceful, you know. No one ringing me about a missing cage.
Lewis: Ha. Yeah, see, that's why I like being my own boss. Nobody ringing me. Well, clients, but I just don't answer sometimes.
Luke: Bet they love that.
Lewis: They get over it. Do you play FC, the PlayStation one?
Luke: Yeah, online with a couple of mates. I'm rubbish though, to be fair.
Lewis: We should get a game in, mate, I'll stick you on—

=== CALL C0017 ===
Tracey: Hiya! Oh, it's you, the Spurs one. Can you hear me?
Lewis: Yeah, yeah, all good. Alright? I'm Lewis.
Tracey: Tracey. I recognised the shirt off your photo. My brother'd have words, he's Walsall through and through.
Lewis: Walsall? Fair play, mate. Someone's gotta support 'em.
Tracey: Oi! Cheeky. So what is it you do, Lewis?
Lewis: I've got my own business, tiling. Bathrooms, kitchens, floors, all that. Out Bishop's Stortford way.
Tracey: Oh, handy. Is that full-time then?
Lewis: Erm, yeah, sort of. Depends on the week, you know. Some weeks it's mental, some weeks it's a bit quieter. I kind of pick and choose.
Tracey: Must be nice, picking and choosing. I'd love that. I'm a fitness instructor at a leisure centre, but it's all sessional, so I take what they give me really.
Lewis: Leisure centre? I play five-a-side at ours every Wednesday.
Tracey: Course you do. Do you have a pint after?
Lewis: Ha, how'd you know?
Tracey: 'Cause that's every one of 'em at mine. They come off the pitch, straight in the bar. And then they wonder why their hamstrings go. Do you warm up?
Lewis: Warm up? Erm. We sort of kick it about a bit first. That counts, yeah?
Tracey: No, it doesn't! I'm telling you straight, you want to be doing proper stretches. Especially kneeling on floors all day. Do you wear knee pads?
Lewis: Sometimes. When I remember. My knees are already starting to go, I'm not gonna lie. Thirty-four and I sound like a bag of crisps getting up off the floor.
Tracey: Well, there you go. Wear the pads. And do some squats, proper ones, it builds the muscle round the knee. I get people in for inductions and I show 'em that first thing.
Lewis: I do go the gym. In phases, like. I'll go every day for three weeks, then nothing for two months.
Tracey: Ha, you and half of Walsall. January it's heaving, February it's me and the cleaner.
Lewis: That's literally me. January I'm a machine.
Tracey: Mm. So do you live round there then, Bishop's Stortford?
Lewis: Yeah. I'm back at my mum and dad's at the minute, just while I save up, you know. Get a deposit together.
Tracey: Oh, that's sensible. Nothing wrong with that. Does your mum feed you?
Lewis: Every night, mate. Roast on a Sunday as well. Can't complain.
Tracey: Lucky. I'm the one doing the feeding in our house, I've got a sixteen-year-old. I batch cook on a Sunday, chilli, spag bol, and it's gone by Wednesday. He'll have his tea and then he's back in the fridge an hour later.
Lewis: Ha, sounds like me at sixteen. Sounds like me now, to be fair.
Tracey: Your poor mum. Do you get away much, holidays and that?
Lewis: Yeah, Marbella last summer with the lads. Did Benidorm for a stag an' all. You can't beat it really, flights from Stansted are like forty quid if you book early.
Tracey: Benidorm! I went twice in my twenties. Never again though, I'm too old for it now. We go to the same caravan park in North Wales every year, near Towyn. My mum, my sister, the kids.
Lewis: Wales? Does it not just rain?
Tracey: Course it rains, that's half the fun. You sit in the caravan with a brew and play cards. Kieran pretends he hates it but he's down the arcades every night.
Lewis: Fair enough. I dunno, I'd want a pool bar, me.
Tracey: You'd be stood in the rain with a pint by the end of the week, I'll bet you—

=== CALL C0018 ===
Luke: Hello? Hi.
Maricel: Hi. Hello. I'm Maricel.
Luke: Luke. Sorry, can you say your name again? Just so I get it right.
Maricel: Maricel. Like Mari, then cel.
Luke: Maricel. Got it. Sorry.
Maricel: No, it's fine, everyone asks. Erm, so what do you do, Luke?
Luke: I'm a shift manager at a parcel depot. Basingstoke. Early shift.
Maricel: Oh, okay. How early is early?
Luke: Half five start. So I'm up about quarter to five.
Maricel: Oh God. I couldn't. I'm knackered after a normal Saturday shift.
Luke: You get used to it. Sort of. Yeah. What about you?
Maricel: I'm a pharmacy technician. In a community pharmacy in Leyton. Checking prescriptions, care home medicines, that kind of thing.
Luke: Oh right. My mum works on reception at a GP surgery. She's always moaning about the repeat prescriptions.
Maricel: Yes! Honestly, before a bank holiday it's chaos. Everyone remembers on the Thursday that they've got two tablets left, and the surgery hasn't sent it over, and then it's us they shout at. Not your mum, I'm sure she's lovely.
Luke: She'd say the same about you lot, to be fair. It's always someone else's fault in the middle, isn't it.
Maricel: Mm. Exactly.
Luke: Bit like the depot. If a parcel goes missing, it's always the shift before.
Maricel: Ha. And is it, though?
Luke: Sometimes it's mine. I'll own up if it is. Yeah.
Maricel: That's good. A lot of people don't. Erm, do you like it? Being the manager?
Luke: Erm. Most of it. I like the people, I've got a good team. I don't like the bit where you've got to push 'em harder for targets, especially near Christmas. Peak season's horrible. I don't really sleep much in November, to be honest.
Maricel: That sounds really stressful.
Luke: Yeah. It's alright. That's about it really.
Maricel: Do you do anything to switch off?
Luke: Fishing, mostly. Carp. I sit by a lake all day on a Saturday and nobody can get hold of me. Caught a decent one last weekend actually.
Maricel: I sort of get that. I do pottery, on the wheel. It's similar, maybe. You can't look at your phone with clay all over your hands. You just have to sit with it for two hours and not think about work.
Luke: Yeah, that's it. That's kind of the same thing, isn't it. Hannah, my girlfriend, she thinks fishing's boring.
Maricel: My partner thinks pottery is just me making very expensive mugs. Which, to be fair, it is.
Luke: Ha. Do you go away much? Holidays and that?
Maricel: Erm, Manila every other year, my family's there. And city breaks sometimes. But honestly, I'm terrible with flying. I plan everything weeks ahead, I check the gate three times, I don't sleep the night before.
Luke: Oh, me too. Hannah laughs at me. I like everything booked months in advance, and I'm at the airport like three hours early.
Maricel: Three hours is normal!
Luke: That's what I keep telling her. We only go Tenerife, it's four hours, and I'm still—

Lewis: Yeah, try telling the grout that. Took me twice as long. Charged her for it, mind.

Lewis: Lisbon. Is that Portugal, yeah? I've only done the Algarve. Albufeira, with the lads.

Lewis: Ha, yeah, bit different. Didn't see many walls. Saw a lot of the pool bar.
Maricel: Erm, so are you busy, with the business?

Maricel: That's good, that you don't have to advertise. I sell a few mugs on Instagram, but honestly, it's so much work. Taking the photos, the posting, the packaging. You make maybe five pounds a mug after everything.
Lewis: Five quid? You want to charge more. Have you seen what they sell mugs for in them fancy shops? Thirty quid, some of 'em. Just price it for whoever's buying.
Maricel: Erm, I don't know. I don't want it to be only for rich people.
Lewis: Nah, I'm just saying. People pay for handmade, don't they.
Maricel: Mm. Maybe. Do you live in Bishop's Stortford?
Lewis: Yeah. Back at my parents' for a bit, just while I save up. It's twenty minutes from Stansted, so that's a bonus.
Maricel: I'm in Walthamstow. The overground's rammed every morning. I'd love twenty minutes from anywhere.
Lewis: Ha, yeah, the M11's no better, mate. Sat on it for forty minutes Tuesday.
Maricel: So, erm, what do you do when you're not working?
Lewis: Football, mostly. Spurs, five-a-side on a Wednesday, bit of FC on the PlayStation. Golf with my dad sometimes, but I'm rubbish, I just get wound up.
Maricel: I don't really know anything about football, honestly. I couldn't name a Spurs player.
Lewis: You've heard of Harry Kane, though, surely?
Maricel: Yes, okay, I know Harry Kane. Isn't he—

Tracey: Mm. So do you live round there then, Bishop's Stortford?
Lewis: Yeah. I'm back at my mum and dad's at the minute, just while I save up, you know. Get a deposit together.
Tracey: Oh, that's sensible. Nothing wrong with that. Does your mum feed you?
Lewis: Every night, mate. Roast on a Sunday as well. Can't complain.
Tracey: Lucky. I'm the one doing the feeding in our house, I've got a sixteen-year-old. I batch cook on a Sunday, chilli, spag bol, and it's gone by Wednesday. He'll have his tea and then he's back in the fridge an hour later.
Lewis: Ha, sounds like me at sixteen. Sounds like me now, to be fair.
Tracey: Your poor mum. Do you get away much, holidays and that?
Lewis: Yeah, Marbella last summer with the lads. Did Benidorm for a stag an' all. You can't beat it really, flights from Stansted are like forty quid if you book early.
Tracey: Benidorm! I went twice in my twenties. Never again though, I'm too old for it now. We go to the same caravan park in North Wales every year, near Towyn. My mum, my sister, the kids.
Lewis: Wales? Does it not just rain?
Tracey: Course it rains, that's half the fun. You sit in the caravan with a brew and play cards. Kieran pretends he hates it but he's down the arcades every night.
Lewis: Fair enough. I dunno, I'd want a pool bar, me.
Tracey: You'd be stood in the rain with a pint by the end of the week, I'll bet you—
calls.C0018:
Luke: Hello? Hi.
Maricel: Hi. Hello. I'm Maricel.
Luke: Luke. Sorry, can you say your name again? Just so I get it right.
Maricel: Maricel. Like Mari, then cel.
Luke: Maricel. Got it. Sorry.
Maricel: No, it's fine, everyone asks. Erm, so what do you do, Luke?
Luke: I'm a shift manager at a parcel depot. Basingstoke. Early shift.
Maricel: Oh, okay. How early is early?
Luke: Half five start. So I'm up about quarter to five.
Maricel: Oh God. I couldn't. I'm knackered after a normal Saturday shift.
Luke: You get used to it. Sort of. Yeah. What about you?
Maricel: I'm a pharmacy technician. In a community pharmacy in Leyton. Checking prescriptions, care home medicines, that kind of thing.
Luke: Oh right. My mum works on reception at a GP surgery. She's always moaning about the repeat prescriptions.
Maricel: Yes! Honestly, before a bank holiday it's chaos. Everyone remembers on the Thursday that they've got two tablets left, and the surgery hasn't sent it over, and then it's us they shout at. Not your mum, I'm sure she's lovely.
Luke: She'd say the same about you lot, to be fair. It's always someone else's fault in the middle, isn't it.
Maricel: Mm. Exactly.
Luke: Bit like the depot. If a parcel goes missing, it's always the shift before.
Maricel: Ha. And is it, though?
Luke: Sometimes it's mine. I'll own up if it is. Yeah.
Maricel: That's good. A lot of people don't. Erm, do you like it? Being the manager?
Luke: Erm. Most of it. I like the people, I've got a good team. I don't like the bit where you've got to push 'em harder for targets, especially near Christmas. Peak season's horrible. I don't really sleep much in November, to be honest.
Maricel: That sounds really stressful.
Luke: Yeah. It's alright. That's about it really.
Maricel: Do you do anything to switch off?
Luke: Fishing, mostly. Carp. I sit by a lake all day on a Saturday and nobody can get hold of me. Caught a decent one last weekend actually.
Maricel: I sort of get that. I do pottery, on the wheel. It's similar, maybe. You can't look at your phone with clay all over your hands. You just have to sit with it for two hours and not think about work.
Luke: Yeah, that's it. That's kind of the same thing, isn't it. Hannah, my girlfriend, she thinks fishing's boring.
Maricel: My partner thinks pottery is just me making very expensive mugs. Which, to be fair, it is.
Luke: Ha. Do you go away much? Holidays and that?
Maricel: Erm, Manila every other year, my family's there. And city breaks sometimes. But honestly, I'm terrible with flying. I plan everything weeks ahead, I check the gate three times, I don't sleep the night before.
Luke: Oh, me too. Hannah laughs at me. I like everything booked months in advance, and I'm at the airport like three hours early.
Maricel: Three hours is normal!
Luke: That's what I keep telling her. We only go Tenerife, it's four hours, and I'm still—
calls.C0019:
Tracey: Hiya! Oh, it's the fishing man. Can you hear me?
Luke: Hi, yeah. Yeah, I can hear you. I'm Luke.
Tracey: Tracey. I said to myself when I saw your photo, he's got all the gear like my brother. He's got a shed full of rods and boxes, his wife won't go in there.
Luke: Ha. Yeah, that's the spare room for me. Hannah's given up on it, to be fair.
Tracey: Is that your girlfriend? Hannah?
Luke: Yeah. Six years. She's a dental nurse.
Tracey: Oh, lovely. So go on, what do you do? Sorry, I've been asking everyone that, I'm like a broken record.
Luke: No, it's fine. I'm a shift manager at a parcel depot. Early shift, about forty staff.
Tracey: Early as in what?
Luke: I'm in for half five.
Tracey: Oh, you poor thing. I thought I had it bad. My first aqua's at seven and the pool's always freezing. I'm in there going "keep moving, keep moving", and it's 'cause I'm cold, not them.
Luke: Ha. You teach in the water?
Tracey: Aqua aerobics, circuits, a seated class for the older ones. Fitness instructor, at a leisure centre in Walsall. I'm sessional, though, so I'm forever chasing a few more hours. I'd love a proper contract, just to know where I am every month, you know?
Luke: Yeah. I get that. Knowing what's coming in. We're saving for a deposit, and every time we get a bit closer, prices go up again round us. Basingstoke's not even that posh, but it's still mental.
Tracey: It's the same everywhere, bab. Sorry, I call everyone that at work. I rent off the housing association, and I'm just glad it's a fair rent, honestly.
Luke: No, you're alright.
Tracey: Do you get tired, the early starts? I'd be dead by Thursday.
Luke: Wednesday, usually. I'm knackered by Wednesday. And it gets worse coming up to Christmas, peak season. That's when I sort of don't sleep. Lot of pressure on numbers, and I don't like pushing the lads harder than is fair. So the fishing's kind of my reset button.
Tracey: That makes sense. I've got my walking group Sunday mornings, up Barr Beacon. Same thing really, you get to the top and you can't worry about nothing, you're too out of breath.
Luke: Ha, yeah.
Tracey: Did you talk to the Spurs lad? Lewis?
Luke: Yeah, first round. He seemed alright. Normal bloke.
Tracey: He told me he warms up for five-a-side by kicking a ball about. I told him straight, that's not a warm-up.
Luke: I used to play. Packed it in after my knee twinged.
Tracey: Did you do any stretching before?
Luke: Erm. No. Not really.
Tracey: There you go then! You lot. What do you do for your tea of a night, do you cook?
Luke: When I'm on earlies I do dinner, yeah. Spag bol, chilli, roast chicken. Nothing fancy. And then Friday's a Chinese, same order every time.
Tracey: Same as me! Chippy on a Friday, and if it's a curry I always have the korma. My sister says I'm boring. I say I know what I like.
Luke: That's what I say. Why change it if it's good.
Tracey: Exactly. My lad Kieran, he's sixteen, he'll eat anything though. I've got to get him to football tonight and he'll want feeding before and after.
Luke: Does he play for a team?
Tracey: Under-seventeens, local club. He's decent, actually. I'm stood on the side every Saturday in the cold with a flask going—
calls.C0020:
Lewis: Alright? Can you hear me, yeah?
Maricel: Hi. Yes, I can hear you. I'm Maricel.
Lewis: Lewis. Nice one. So, er, what d'you do?
Maricel: I'm a pharmacy technician. In Leyton.
Lewis: Oh, right. My mum works at a GP surgery. Practice manager.
Maricel: Oh, okay. So she knows all about the prescription side, then.
Lewis: Yeah, she moans about it, to be fair. Every dinner it's someone who's shouted at the receptionist.
Maricel: That happens to us as well. It's always the person in the middle. And you, what do you do?
Lewis: I've got my own business. Tiling. Bathrooms, kitchen floors, splashbacks, that kind of thing.
Maricel: Oh, tiling. That's actually interesting. I do pottery, so I'm sort of obsessed with glazes. Do you ever do handmade tiles? Or is it mostly the big shiny ones?
Lewis: Mostly the big ones, yeah. Porcelain, big format, people love it now. Had one woman wanted handmade Moroccan ones once. Nightmare. None of 'em are the same size, you can't get your lines straight.
Maricel: But that's the point of them! They're meant to be a bit uneven.
Lewis: Yeah, try telling the grout that. Took me twice as long. Charged her for it, mind.
Maricel: Ha. Fair enough, I suppose. When we went to Lisbon, all the buildings had those painted blue tiles. Azulejos. I spent the whole time taking photos of walls. My partner thought I'd gone mad.
Lewis: Lisbon. Is that Portugal, yeah? I've only done the Algarve. Albufeira, with the lads.
Maricel: Mm. Different sort of trip, maybe.
Lewis: Ha, yeah, bit different. Didn't see many walls. Saw a lot of the pool bar.
Maricel: Erm, so are you busy, with the business?
Lewis: Yeah, it's alright. Bits and bobs. I sort of pick my jobs. Word of mouth mostly, my dad knows a lot of people.
Maricel: That's good, that you don't have to advertise. I sell a few mugs on Instagram, but honestly, it's so much work. Taking the photos, the posting, the packaging. You make maybe five pounds a mug after everything.
Lewis: Five quid? You want to charge more. Have you seen what they sell mugs for in them fancy shops? Thirty quid, some of 'em. Just price it for whoever's buying.
Maricel: Erm, I don't know. I don't want it to be only for rich people.
Lewis: Nah, I'm just saying. People pay for handmade, don't they.
Maricel: Mm. Maybe. Do you live in Bishop's Stortford?
Lewis: Yeah. Back at my parents' for a bit, just while I save up. It's twenty minutes from Stansted, so that's a bonus.
Maricel: I'm in Walthamstow. The overground's rammed every morning. I'd love twenty minutes from anywhere.
Lewis: Ha, yeah, the M11's no better, mate. Sat on it for forty minutes Tuesday.
Maricel: So, erm, what do you do when you're not working?
Lewis: Football, mostly. Spurs, five-a-side on a Wednesday, bit of FC on the PlayStation. Golf with my dad sometimes, but I'm rubbish, I just get wound up.
Maricel: I don't really know anything about football, honestly. I couldn't name a Spurs player.
Lewis: You've heard of Harry Kane, though, surely?
Maricel: Yes, okay, I know Harry Kane. Isn't he—

C0015.line_text: So is that all week then, the pharmacy?
C0015.what: A tall teenage boy in a hoodie walks through the kitchen behind Tracey. He opens the fridge, takes out a carton and leaves the frame. Tracey doesn't turn round.
